archetype.name: Playoff Team (opportunistic, two-way efficient)
archetype.definition: A second-year Coen team with a top-10 offense by EPA and a defense that wins on takeaways and red-zone stops, good enough to win the division comfortably but leaning on margins that won't all hold.

report.headline: A contender's efficiency, but a defense living on takeaways and red-zone stops
report.take:
This is the second act of the Liam Coen era, and it looks more honest than the first. Last year's 13-4 team finished first in the league in wins over expected (3.87), so the record outran a point differential that was already good. Through four games in 2026 the margin has caught up with the reputation: +12.8 points per game (2nd), net EPA 2nd, and only 0.76 wins over expected. The offense ranks 7th in EPA and is balanced. Pass EPA is 8th and rush EPA 5th, with a pass rate over expected near zero (-0.5), so Coen isn't forcing the game in either direction.

The engine is the turnover column. Jacksonville is +1.5 per game, best in the league: 8 takeaways against 2 giveaways, with Lawrence turning it over once or less every week. The run game is better than its line. Yards before contact are 1.66 (30th), yet run success is 46.3% (5th) and rush EPA 5th, which says Bhayshul Tuten (60 carries) is creating after contact rather than walking through holes. Lawrence is averaging about 211 passing yards on a spread tree, with Parker Washington (26 targets) ahead of Brenton Strange, Jakobi Meyers and Brian Thomas Jr. It is efficient rather than explosive.

The numbers hide a team that is being outgained. The Jaguars allow 355.3 yards per game (26th) and gain 317.8 (18th), a deficit of about 37 yards a game, while winning by nearly 13 points. The gap comes from three things that rarely all persist. Takeaways produce short fields, opponents score touchdowns on only 28.6% of red-zone trips (2nd), and third downs are at 32.6% (5th). The underneath coverage is the best in football by EPA on short throws. Deep balls are another story: deep EPA 22nd, explosive pass rate 24th, and Cincinnati threw for 428 yards in Week 4. The pass rush (16% pressure rate, 25th) isn't covering for it. Because EPA counts turnovers, even the net EPA ranking is partly the takeaways talking. On offense, Lawrence is hit on 19.3% of dropbacks (29th), and the Cincinnati win came with 4 sacks and 125 penalty yards.

Where this goes: the schedule is soft enough to absorb regression. Four of the remaining games are against Houston and Tennessee, both 0-4. Only Baltimore, Chicago and Dallas bring top-10 offenses, and all three are road games. The defense will give back points as the takeaway rate and red-zone luck normalize, and the secondary is thinning (Montaric Brown out, Eric Murray in concussion territory). The offense is sturdy enough, though, that this projects as a division winner rather than a fade candidate.

strengths.title: Best turnover margin in football
strengths.body: Eight takeaways against two giveaways is the biggest single driver of the +12.8 point differential. The giveaway half is the sturdier piece because it reflects Lawrence's ball security in a run-supported offense. The takeaway half will cool. Turnover margin was also 3rd last season, so this is partly a repeatable trait, not pure luck.

strengths.title: Run game beats its blocking
strengths.body: Rush EPA is 5th and run success 46.3% even though backs get only 1.66 yards before contact (30th). That points to Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr. winning after contact and to good short-yardage execution (90.9% conversion, 2nd). Production that comes from the runners rather than the line is somewhat fragile, but it has held across all four games, with 95 or more rushing yards every week.

strengths.title: Elite underneath and situational defense
strengths.body: No defense is better against short passes by EPA, which is why third downs (32.6%, 5th) and red-zone trips (28.6% TDs, 2nd) die. The short-pass coverage is a real structural strength. The red-zone rate is too extreme to last, and it will drift toward average.

concerns.title: Points allowed flatter a leaky defense
concerns.body: Allowing 13.3 points (2nd) while giving up 355.3 yards (26th) is a mismatch that resolves toward the yardage. The weakness is the deep ball: deep EPA 22nd, explosive pass rate 24th, and 428 passing yards allowed at Cincinnati. A better quarterback who avoids turnovers will score on this unit.

concerns.title: No pass rush, thinning secondary
concerns.body: A 16% pressure rate (25th) means the coverage has to hold up on its own. That coverage is now down starting corner Montaric Brown (67% of snaps) and possibly safety Eric Murray (76%), who left Week 4 with a concussion. This is a real flaw in the build, made worse by injuries, not a cost of some other strength.

concerns.title: Lawrence takes too many hits
concerns.body: Opponents hit Lawrence on 19.3% of dropbacks (29th), and the sack rate sits at 7% (21st). It peaked with 4 sacks at Cincinnati, the best defense the Jaguars have faced. Average-length dropbacks (2.745 seconds) suggest the problem is the line, not the quarterback holding the ball, and it is the likeliest path to the offense stalling against good fronts.

trend.note: Two blowouts at home (by 24 and 29), a flat road loss in Denver where the passing game posted negative EPA, then a road upset of Cincinnati as an underdog. Efficiency has been strong in three of four games, and the Week 4 win came against the best opponent so far.

nextGame.headline: Jaguars host an Eagles team stripped of weapons and protection
nextGame.body:
Philadelphia arrives at 2-2 with the 31st-ranked net EPA, an offense 29th in EPA by play-by-play, and no covers in four games. Its defense is the ideal opponent for Jacksonville's biggest offensive weakness. The Eagles generate pressure on just 11.2% of dropbacks (31st) and the league's lowest hit rate, so Lawrence should get the clean pockets he hasn't had. The Eagles also miss 14.1% of tackles (31st) and rank 29th against the run, which suits a Jaguars ground game that lives on yards after contact. Where Philadelphia is solid is deep (6th in deep EPA allowed), so expect Jacksonville's methodical, short-area and run-heavy version rather than shot plays.

The injury report is lopsided. Philadelphia is without DeVonta Smith, Dallas Goedert, Hollywood Brown and Lane Johnson. Center Cam Jurgens is in the concussion protocol, Saquon Barkley is week-to-week with a hamstring, and Tank Bigsby is headed to IR. On defense, Zack Baun and Marcus Epps are out, with Quinyon Mitchell and Jonathan Greenard questionable. Jacksonville's own concerns are in the secondary: Montaric Brown and Christian Braswell are out, and Eric Murray and Caleb Ransaw are questionable. That thin back end is the one place a depleted Eagles passing game could still find a play.

keyMatchups.title: Tuten against the league's worst tacklers
keyMatchups.body: Jacksonville's run game produces after contact, and Philadelphia misses tackles at the second-worst rate in the league while ranking 29th in rush EPA allowed. This is the cleanest edge on the board. A steady ground game also lets Jacksonville control the clock and keep the ball away from an offense that already struggles to move.

keyMatchups.title: Patched Eagles line vs. coverage
keyMatchups.body: Philadelphia already allows sacks on 8.7% of dropbacks (27th), with a long time to throw of 3.215 seconds, and is now without a 100%-snap tackle. Jacksonville doesn't pressure much, but its sticky underneath coverage forces exactly the long-developing dropbacks that produce sacks and turnovers behind a weakened line.

keyMatchups.title: Eagles' special teams and fourth downs
keyMatchups.body: Philadelphia's main ways to swing a game are special teams (4.0 EPA per game, 4th) and going for it on every fourth down so far. Those are the backdoor-cover risks against a big spread. Jacksonville has never gone for it on fourth down this year, which makes the Eagles the more aggressive side in a close game.

nextGame.watch: Whether Jacksonville's depleted secondary gives up a deep completion. It is the only realistic path for a shorthanded Philadelphia offense to keep this within a touchdown.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is the sustainable part. Top-10 EPA in both phases, low giveaways and a run game that has produced every week should keep scoring in the mid-20s, especially with six of 12 remaining games against the Houston, Tennessee and Indianapolis defenses, none ranked better than 21st. The defense is where regression lands. A red-zone touchdown rate near 29% and a takeaway pace of two per game won't hold, and once they fade, the yardage allowed (26th) starts turning into points. Expect points allowed to climb toward the high teens, more so if the secondary injuries linger.

Even with that give-back, the path to the division is wide open. Jacksonville leads Indianapolis by a game, Houston and Tennessee are both winless, and those four division games account for a third of what's left. The real tests are road trips to Baltimore, Chicago and Dallas, all top-10 offenses that can exploit the deep-ball weakness. Those games will decide whether this is a home-playoff-game team or merely a division winner.
swingFactors: Pass protection against Baltimore, Chicago and Dallas

bets.reason: Philadelphia scores 18.8 per game with a full roster and ranks 29th in offensive EPA. It is now missing Smith, Goedert, Brown and Lane Johnson, with Jurgens and Barkley uncertain. Jacksonville allows 13.3 points and opponents score touchdowns on just 28.6% of red-zone trips.

The net EPA gap is extreme (2nd vs. 31st), Jacksonville has covered three of four, Philadelphia has covered none, and the injury report tilts heavily one way. It's only a lean because 7 is a key number and Philadelphia's 4th-ranked special teams can produce a backdoor cover.

Three of Jacksonville's four games went under, with combined scoring averaging about 39 points. A shorthanded Eagles offense plus a Jaguars game plan built on the run and clock control points the same way. The risk is Jacksonville's defense giving up chunk plays, which keeps this from being a stronger play.

confidence.note: Four-game sample with a turnover-heavy margin, but the profile matches last season's and the schedule is soft.
